claims.text: The tested material is polycrystalline, near-equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The proposed multiscale machine-learning model will explicitly incorporate measured oxygen content, defect states, interstitial-oxygen distributions, and temperature-dependent scattering rates.
Interstitial oxygen causes local lattice distortions in HfNbTaTiZr.
Interstitial oxygen creates additional electronic-scattering centers in HfNbTaTiZr.
Defect-related energy states and impurity-induced scattering materially affect the alloy's electrical conductivity.
Temperature-dependent scattering contributions are relevant in both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
A physics-informed ML model that includes impurities and defects will capture real scattering contributions better than idealized defect-free models.
The proposed model will produce narrower conductivity residuals than conventional defect-free analytical predictions.
The model will predict electrical conductivity within ±5% of measurements across both specified temperature regimes.
The ±5% conductivity accuracy will hold on specimens or data withheld from model training.
Standard defect-free analytical methods typically deviate from measured conductivity by at least 15%.
The analytical-model errors are especially large at high impurity levels and over wide temperature ranges.
The proposed model is applicable to near-equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen from 0 to 1200 K.
Applicability outside the stated composition, oxygen content, and temperature limits is unverified.
Prediction accuracy depends on consistent defect characterization and sufficiently complete training data over the full temperature range.
The hypothesis is falsified if conductivity error exceeds ±5% for more than 25% of held-out test points.

contradictions.description: The conditions and predicted outcome cover two disjoint regimes, 0–200 K and 300–1200 K, whereas the boundary claims validity continuously from 0 to 1200 K, implicitly including the unaddressed 200–300 K interval.
